error_modes.label: Course deviation on the published SID radials

texts.0: SP, due to an uncontrolled bank angle in the turn to the departure course, did not intercept and hold the published radial and allowed course deviation to exceed 8 degrees with the CDI at full deflection. The divergence from the SID track was not recognized on the navigation display and continued to increase. IP intervention on the controls was required to regain the published course.
texts.1: SP, due to a late intercept turn at the departure fix, overshot the published radial and allowed course deviation to reach the 8 degree limit. The developing trend on the CDI was not detected, and the intercept back to course was started only after repeated verbal prompting from the IP. Course was recaptured well after the point at which the correction was required.
texts.2: SP, due to an imprecise wind correction angle on the climb-out radial, drifted off the published course by between 5 and 8 degrees. The deviation was recognized on the CDI while it was still developing and SP applied a measured intercept heading without IP input. Course was re-established on the SID radial and held from that point to the departure fix.
texts.3: SP intercepted and maintained the published SID radials with course deviation held within 5 degrees throughout the departure. Wind correction was established early and adjusted in small increments, keeping the CDI close to center. Each fix was tracked without overshoot.
texts.4: SP flew the published SID track with course deviation held to approximately 2 degrees, with the CDI effectively centered from the first radial intercept to the departure fix. The wind correction angle was set on the initial turn and required no further adjustment. Intercepts were completed without overshoot or subsequent hunting.
texts.marginal: SP kept course deviation inside the 5 degree standard, but the CDI was allowed to work out close to that limit before each correction was applied. Corrections were made as single large heading changes rather than early small ones, producing a slow oscillation about the published radial. The parameter is within standards; SP is expected to set the wind correction angle earlier and correct in smaller increments on subsequent sorties.

texts_at.0: With the IP calling the intercept turn at the departure fix and demonstrating the correction on the CDI, SP flew the intercept back to course on the call given. The developing trend on the CDI after a late intercept has not yet been learned to detect independently, so the correction is still prompted rather than started on the trend itself. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin detecting the CDI trend at the departure fix without it being prompted.
texts_at.1: SP recaptured the published radial only after repeated verbal prompting from the IP, with course deviation reaching the 8 degree limit, because the developing trend had not been detected on the CDI after a late intercept turn at the departure fix. The course was regained once the prompting had been given. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to detect the CDI trend at the departure fix without needing it prompted.
texts_at.2: SP applied a measured intercept heading without IP input after an imprecise wind correction angle let the aircraft drift roughly 7 degrees off the published course, re-establishing the SID radial from that point to the departure fix. The correction came from recognizing the developing trend on the CDI. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to set the wind correction angle at the intercept so the drift does not develop.
texts_at.3: SP intercepted and maintained the published SID radials with course deviation held within 5 degrees throughout the departure, establishing the wind correction early and adjusting it in small increments so the CDI stayed close to center. One intercept was tracked a touch wider than the others before settling on the radial. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to bring every intercept to the same tightness as the best one.

texts_above.1: SP recaptured the published radial after the departure fix, containing course deviation to the 8 degree limit. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP held course deviation between 5 and 8 degrees, applying a measured intercept heading without IP input after an imprecise wind correction angle let the aircraft drift off the published course. The SID radial was re-established and held from that point to the departure fix. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good course-deviation correction on the SID radials.
texts_above.3: SP intercepted and maintained the published SID radials with course deviation held within 5 degrees on every segment, setting the wind correction angle early and adjusting it in small increments so the CDI stayed close to center. No intercept on the departure produced an overshoot. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed course-deviation correction on the SID radials.
texts_above.4: SP flew the published SID track with course deviation held to approximately 2 degrees, the CDI effectively centered from the first radial intercept to the departure fix, and the wind correction angle set on the initial turn requiring no further adjustment. Every intercept was completed without overshoot or subsequent hunting. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent course-deviation correction on the SID radials.

error_modes.label: Knowledge and sequence of the published departure (MAIP)

texts.0: SP, due to insufficient study of the published departure in MAIP, did not know the SID sequence and flew an initial heading and climb segment other than the published one. The required turn point was passed without action and the aircraft continued outside the departure track. IP assistance was required to state the procedure and to fly the aircraft back onto the published routing.
texts.1: SP, due to reliance on memory instead of the departure plate, applied the SID segments out of sequence and started the turn at the wrong fix. The procedure was reconstructed only after the IP prompted the next step verbally, and the aircraft was by then at the outer edge of the departure track. The remaining segments were flown correctly but with continuous prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to an incomplete review of the departure plate before takeoff, hesitated at the transition between the first and second SID segments and began the turn late. SP identified the omission from the plate and executed the correct segment without IP assistance, keeping the aircraft on the published routing. No further sequencing errors occurred for the remainder of the departure.
texts.3: SP knew the published departure as described in MAIP and executed each segment in the correct sequence without IP assistance. Headings, turn points and altitude restrictions were applied at the published positions. The departure was flown to the transition fix as briefed.
texts.4: SP executed the published departure flawlessly and without IP assistance, anticipating every segment change before it was reached. The plate was used as confirmation rather than as a source of the sequence, and each restriction was met with the aircraft already configured for the next segment. The departure required no correction of any kind.
texts.marginal: SP executed the published departure without IP assistance, but the sequence was recalled a step at a time and each segment change was confirmed on the plate only as it arrived. This left no margin for a clearance amendment and slowed the transitions slightly. Performance meets the standard; SP is expected to arrive at the aircraft with the SID sequence memorized to the level required for anticipation.

texts_at.0: With the IP naming the next SID segment at each transition, SP flew the segment named from the departure plate. The sequence of the published departure has not yet been learned well enough to fly from memory, so each segment is still supplied by the IP rather than checked on the plate independently. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin checking the plate at each transition without the next segment being named.
texts_at.1: SP reconstructed the SID sequence only after the IP prompted the next step verbally, with the aircraft by then up to 8 degrees off the published track, at the outer edge of the standard, because the segments had been applied out of order from memory rather than from the departure plate. The remaining segments were flown correctly once the prompting had begun. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to check the plate at each transition without needing the next step prompted.
texts_at.2: SP identified an incomplete review of the departure plate at the transition between the first and second SID segments, executed the correct segment without IP assistance and kept the aircraft on the published routing with course deviation held to about 7 degrees. No further sequencing error occurred for the rest of the departure. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to complete the plate review before the first transition so no hesitation develops there.
texts_at.3: SP knew the published departure as described in MAIP and executed each segment in the correct sequence without IP assistance, applying headings, turn points and altitude restrictions at the published positions with course deviation held within 5 degrees throughout. The sequence was recalled a step at a time and confirmed on the plate as each segment arrived, rather than ahead of it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to arrive with the sequence memorized well enough to anticipate the next segment.

texts_above.1: SP reconstructed the SID sequence and flew the remaining segments correctly once each transition had been checked against the plate. That correction came after a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP executed the SID segment correctly without IP assistance, having identified an incomplete plate review at the transition between the first and second segments and closing the gap before the aircraft left the published routing. No further sequencing error appeared for the rest of the departure. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid departure-sequence knowledge.
texts_above.3: SP knew the published departure as described in MAIP and executed every segment in the correct sequence without IP assistance, applying headings, turn points and altitude restrictions at the published positions on the whole departure. The plate was used to confirm the sequence rather than to recall it. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate departure-sequence knowledge.
texts_above.4: SP executed the published departure flawlessly and without IP assistance, anticipating every segment change before it was reached and meeting each restriction with the aircraft already configured for the next segment. The departure required no correction of any kind. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary departure-sequence knowledge.

error_modes.label: Basic Control Standards during the climb on the SID

texts.0: SP, due to an untrimmed aircraft after the climb was established, did not maintain the departure profile within Basic Control Standards, with airspeed and pitch attitude varying continuously through the climb. The published altitude restriction was passed without the level-off being started. IP intervention was required to stabilize the aircraft and to comply with the restriction.
texts.1: SP, due to a fixed rather than cyclic instrument cross-check, allowed climb airspeed and heading to reach the limits of Basic Control Standards during the departure. The deviations were corrected only after verbal indication from the IP, and the level-off at the published altitude was begun late. Parameters were restored, but the correction was not initiated by SP.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed trim change after the initial climb was established, allowed climb airspeed and pitch attitude to move beyond the target values while remaining inside the outer control limits. SP identified the trend on the primary flight instruments and re-trimmed to the climb attitude without IP input. The published altitude restriction was then met with a normal level-off.
texts.3: SP maintained the departure profile within Basic Control Standards, holding climb airspeed, heading and attitude at the target values. The aircraft was trimmed for the climb and the instrument cross-check remained cyclic. Published altitude restrictions were met with stabilized level-offs.
texts.4: SP flew the climb on the SID with airspeed, heading and attitude effectively fixed at the target values and the aircraft trimmed hands-off after the initial climb was established. Level-offs at the published restrictions were anticipated and completed without any excursion. Control inputs throughout the departure were small and continuous.
texts.marginal: SP held the departure profile inside Basic Control Standards, but airspeed and attitude required repeated correction because the aircraft was flown out of trim for most of the climb. Each parameter was recovered before it approached the limit, at the cost of continuous attention to control inputs. The item is within standards; SP is expected to trim accurately at the start of the climb so that capacity is available for the navigation task.

texts_at.0: With the IP calling the developing airspeed and heading trends during the climb, SP corrected the parameters named on the departure. The cyclic instrument cross-check needed through a climbing departure has not yet been learned, so trends are still identified by the IP rather than caught on SP's own scan. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to begin keeping the cross-check cyclic through the departure without the deviation being pointed out.
texts_at.1: SP had the deviations corrected only after verbal indication from the IP, with climb airspeed and heading having reached the limits of Basic Control Standards and course deviation reaching 8 degrees on the departure radial, because the instrument cross-check had been fixed rather than cyclic through the departure. The level-off at the published altitude followed once the indication had been given. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to keep the cross-check cyclic without needing the deviation pointed out.
texts_at.2: SP identified a trend on the primary flight instruments and re-trimmed to the climb attitude without IP input, after a delayed trim change let climb airspeed and pitch attitude move beyond the target values and course deviation grow to approximately 7 degrees on the departure radial. The published altitude restriction was then met with a normal level-off. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to re-trim as soon as the climb is established rather than after the target values have drifted.
texts_at.3: SP maintained the departure profile within Basic Control Standards, holding climb airspeed, heading and attitude at the target values with course deviation inside 5 degrees, the aircraft trimmed for the climb and the cross-check kept cyclic. One level-off needed a slightly firmer correction than the others before it stabilized. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to bring every level-off to the same smoothness as the best one.

texts_above.1: SP corrected climb airspeed and heading back inside Basic Control Standards during the departure. The IP's verbal call preceded the correction. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP re-trimmed to the climb attitude without IP input after identifying a trend on the primary flight instruments, recovering climb airspeed and pitch attitude before either left the outer control limits. The published altitude restriction was then met with a normal level-off. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady basic control discipline on the climb.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the departure profile within Basic Control Standards on every segment, holding climb airspeed, heading and attitude at the target values with the aircraft trimmed for the climb and the cross-check kept cyclic throughout. Every published altitude restriction was met with a stabilized level-off. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate basic control discipline on the climb.
texts_above.4: SP flew the climb on the SID with airspeed, heading and attitude effectively fixed at the target values and the aircraft trimmed hands-off after the initial climb was established, anticipating every level-off at the published restrictions with no excursion. Control inputs throughout the departure were small and continuous. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary basic control discipline on the climb.

error_modes.label: Timeliness and quality of track deviation corrections

texts.0: SP, due to misinterpretation of the CDI rate of movement, did not recognize the developing track deviation and applied no correction while the aircraft continued to diverge from the published course. When a correction was finally attempted it was made in the wrong direction and increased the displacement. IP intervention was required to establish an intercept back to the SID track.
texts.1: SP, due to a scan that remained on the attitude and airspeed indications, detected the track deviation only when it had reached the outer limit and then applied an intercept angle large enough to produce an overshoot on the other side. The oscillation about the published course was stopped only after verbal guidance from the IP on the intercept heading to fly. Track was regained late in the departure segment.
texts.2: SP, due to an initially small intercept angle, corrected the track deviation more slowly than the geometry required and the displacement persisted for part of the segment. SP reassessed the closure rate on the CDI, increased the intercept angle and returned the aircraft to the published course without IP input. Subsequent deviations were corrected as soon as they appeared.
texts.3: SP corrected track deviations in a timely manner, applying intercept angles matched to the displacement and the distance remaining to the fix. Corrections were recognized from the CDI trend rather than from full displacement. The aircraft was returned to the published course without overshoot.
texts.4: SP anticipated track deviations from the first movement of the CDI and corrected them before any measurable displacement developed. Intercept angles were proportional and were reduced progressively so that the aircraft rolled out on course each time. No correction required a second input.
texts.marginal: SP corrected every track deviation and kept the aircraft on the published course, but the corrections were consistently started only after the displacement had become clearly visible rather than at the first trend indication. Each correction was therefore larger than necessary and required a follow-up input to settle. Performance is within standards; SP is expected to act on the CDI trend earlier so that a single proportional correction is sufficient.

texts_at.0: With the IP naming the intercept heading to fly back to the published course, SP turned to the heading named. The sizing of an intercept angle to the displacement has not yet been learned, so the heading to fly is still supplied by the IP rather than judged from the displacement seen. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to begin sizing the first intercept angle to the displacement without a second correction being called.
texts_at.1: SP stopped the oscillation about the published course only after verbal guidance from the IP on the intercept heading to fly, because the track deviation had been detected only at the 8 degree outer limit and the resulting intercept angle had produced an overshoot. Track was regained late in the departure segment once the guidance had been given. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to size the first intercept angle to the displacement without needing a second correction called.
texts_at.2: SP reassessed the closure rate on the CDI, increased the intercept angle and returned the aircraft to the published course without IP input, after an initially small intercept angle had let a track deviation of about 7 degrees persist for part of the segment. Subsequent deviations were corrected as soon as they appeared. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to size the first intercept angle to the geometry so a second increase is not needed.
texts_at.3: SP corrected track deviations in a timely manner, holding them inside 5 degrees and applying intercept angles matched to the displacement and the distance remaining to the fix, with corrections recognized from the CDI trend rather than from full displacement. One correction was recognized a little later than the others before the geometry was reassessed. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to recognize every CDI trend at the same point in its development.

texts_above.1: SP stopped the oscillation about the published course and regained track during the departure segment. A verbal call from the IP came before the correction. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP reassessed the closure rate on the CDI and increased the intercept angle without IP input, after an initially small intercept angle had let a track deviation persist briefly, returning the aircraft to the published course before the displacement grew further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound track-deviation correction timing.
texts_above.3: SP corrected every track deviation in a timely manner on the departure, applying intercept angles matched to the displacement and the distance remaining to the fix and recognizing each correction from the CDI trend rather than from full displacement. No correction on the departure needed to be reassessed. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise track-deviation correction timing.
texts_above.4: SP anticipated track deviations from the first movement of the CDI and corrected them before any measurable displacement developed, with intercept angles proportional and reduced progressively so the aircraft rolled out on course every time. No correction required a second input. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate track-deviation correction timing.

error_modes.label: Compliance with ATC instructions during the departure

texts.0: SP, due to an incorrect read-back that was not compared against the clearance received, did not comply with the ATC instruction and continued on the SID routing after being assigned radar vectors. The mismatch between the assigned and the flown heading was not detected. IP intervention was required to query ATC and to fly the assigned heading.
texts.1: SP, due to a read-back made without confirming the assigned altitude, complied with the ATC instruction only after the controller repeated it and the IP prompted verbally. The aircraft continued on the previous clearance until that point. Compliance was eventually achieved but at the limit of the time available.
texts.2: SP, due to attention held on the navigation task, acknowledged the ATC instruction late and started the assigned turn after the expected moment. SP recognized the delay, checked the assigned heading against the read-back and complied without IP assistance. Subsequent instructions were acknowledged and executed promptly.
texts.3: SP complied with all ATC instructions during the departure, reading back each clearance correctly and executing it promptly. Assigned headings and altitudes were cross-checked against the read-back before being flown. No clarification was required from the controller.
texts.4: SP complied with every ATC instruction immediately and accurately, with correct standard read-back on each transmission and the assigned values set on the aircraft before the turn was started. Amendments to the SID routing were absorbed without any interruption to the flight path or to the departure profile. The controller required no repetition or confirmation at any point.
texts.marginal: SP complied with all ATC instructions and read them back correctly, but each read-back was delayed while SP completed the flying task first and the controller had to wait for the acknowledgement. Compliance itself was always achieved within the required time. The item meets the standard; SP is expected to integrate the radio task with the flying task so that acknowledgement is not deferred.

texts_at.0: With the controller repeating the instruction and the IP prompting the read-back, SP complied with the clearance once it had been repeated. The habit of confirming an assigned value in the read-back itself has not yet been built, so compliance still waits for a repeat rather than being confirmed on the first call. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to begin confirming the assigned value in the read-back itself rather than needing a repeat.
texts_at.1: SP complied with the ATC instruction only after the controller repeated it and the IP prompted verbally, with the aircraft continuing on the previous clearance until that point, because the read-back had been made without confirming the assigned altitude. Compliance was achieved once the prompting had been given, at the limit of the time available. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to confirm the assigned value in the read-back itself rather than needing a repeat.
texts_at.2: SP checked the assigned heading against the read-back and complied without IP assistance, after attention held on the navigation task had let the acknowledgement of the ATC instruction run late and the aircraft drift about 6 degrees off the assigned course. Subsequent instructions were acknowledged and executed promptly for the remainder of the departure. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to acknowledge each instruction as soon as it is received rather than after the navigation task is clear.
texts_at.3: SP complied with all ATC instructions during the departure, reading back each clearance correctly and executing it promptly, with assigned headings and altitudes cross-checked against the read-back before being flown and each assigned course then held within 5 degrees. One acknowledgement was made a moment after the navigation task rather than alongside it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to acknowledge every instruction as it arrives regardless of what the navigation task is doing.

texts_above.1: SP complied with the ATC instruction once the controller had repeated it, resuming the assigned clearance. SP corrected after a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP checked the assigned heading against the read-back and complied without IP assistance, catching one acknowledgement that had run late while attention was on the navigation task and closing the gap before the next instruction. Every later instruction was acknowledged and executed promptly. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable ATC-instruction compliance.
texts_above.3: SP complied with every ATC instruction during the departure, reading back each clearance correctly and executing it promptly with assigned headings and altitudes cross-checked against the read-back before being flown. No clarification was required from the controller at any point. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good ATC-instruction compliance.
texts_above.4: SP complied with every ATC instruction immediately and accurately, with correct standard read-back on each transmission and the assigned values set on the aircraft before the turn was started, absorbing amendments to the SID routing without any interruption to the flight path. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior ATC-instruction compliance.

error_modes.label: Navigation aid and avionics setup for the SID

texts.0: SP, due to mode confusion over the selected avionics mode and what it was displaying, flew the departure with the navigation source set to the wrong facility and did not track the published radial at all. The indications presented were accepted without being cross-checked against the departure plate. IP intervention was required to reconfigure the navigation source and to regain the SID track.
texts.1: SP, due to an incorrect assumption about which navigation mode was active, set the course for the second SID segment but left the source on the previous facility, and the error was found only when the IP indicated it verbally. Until that point the aircraft was tracking an indication that did not correspond to the published segment. The setup was corrected and the departure continued at the limit of the assigned track.
texts.2: SP, due to insufficient knowledge of the display hierarchy for the selection made, set the navigation source correctly but selected the course for the next segment late, leaving the intercept information unavailable during part of the turn. SP identified the omission at the mode annunciation, completed the setup and flew the segment without IP input. The remaining segments were set up before each transition.
texts.3: SP set the navigation aids and avionics for each SID segment correctly and in advance, with frequencies, courses and navigation source selected before the segment was reached. The selections were confirmed against the departure plate and the mode annunciations. No setup action was required inside a turn.
texts.4: SP configured the avionics for the entire departure before takeoff and confirmed each selection against the departure plate, so that every segment change required only a course change already pre-set. The active navigation mode was verified at each annunciation, and no indication was accepted without a cross-check. The departure was flown with the correct source displayed at all times.
texts.marginal: SP set the navigation aids and avionics correctly for every SID segment, but the selections were made close to the transition point rather than in advance, and the mode annunciation was checked only after the change. This left the setup competing with the flying task inside the turns. The item is within standards; SP is expected to pre-select and verify each segment well before it is reached.

texts_at.0: With the IP pointing out the navigation source that did not match the published segment, SP corrected the setup indicated. The habit of checking the active avionics mode against the departure plate has not yet been built, so an incorrect assumption about the mode is still found by the IP rather than tested by SP. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin checking the active mode against the departure plate without the error being indicated.
texts_at.1: SP corrected the navigation setup only after the IP indicated the error verbally, with the aircraft tracking an indication that did not correspond to the published segment until that point, because an incorrect assumption about the active avionics mode had been carried into the setup. The departure continued up to 8 degrees off the assigned track, at the limit of the standard, once the setup had been corrected. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to check the active mode against the departure plate before relying on the indication.
texts_at.2: SP identified an omission at the mode annunciation, completed the setup and flew the segment without IP input, after insufficient knowledge of the display hierarchy had left the intercept information unavailable for part of a turn, letting course deviation reach around 7 degrees. The remaining segments were set up before each transition. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to complete each segment's setup before the turn that needs it rather than during the turn.
texts_at.3: SP set the navigation aids and avionics for each SID segment correctly and in advance, with frequencies, courses and navigation source selected before the segment was reached and confirmed against the departure plate and the mode annunciations, so every segment was intercepted with course deviation within 5 degrees. One selection was made a moment closer to the transition than the others. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to set every segment with the same lead time as the earliest one.

texts_above.1: SP corrected the navigation setup and continued the departure on the published segment. The IP's call came first, and the correction followed it. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP completed the setup and flew the segment without IP input, having identified an omission at the mode annunciation after insufficient knowledge of the display hierarchy briefly left the intercept information unavailable. Every remaining segment was set up before its transition. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured navaid and avionics setup for the SID.
texts_above.3: SP set the navigation aids and avionics for every SID segment correctly and in advance, with frequencies, courses and navigation source selected before each segment was reached and confirmed against the departure plate and the mode annunciations. No setup action was required inside a turn on the whole departure. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed navaid and avionics setup for the SID.
texts_above.4: SP configured the avionics for the entire departure before takeoff and confirmed each selection against the departure plate, so every segment change required only a course change already pre-set, with the active navigation mode verified at each annunciation and no indication accepted without a cross-check. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent navaid and avionics setup for the SID.

error_modes.label: Workload management and independence from IP assistance

texts.0: SP, due to task sequencing that concentrated all cockpit workload inside the departure turn, did not execute the climb checks and simultaneously lost control of the navigation task. Neither the checklist nor the SID track was completed without help, and the aircraft continued outside the published routing. IP intervention was required to fly the aircraft while the sequence was reordered.
texts.1: SP, due to workload management that left the climb checklist unfinished before the first altitude restriction, saturated at the transition and stopped flying the departure while working the cockpit tasks. Progress resumed only after the IP prompted the order of actions verbally. The departure was completed, but not without IP assistance as required by the standard.
texts.2: SP, due to failure to shed the secondary cockpit task when workload increased at the segment change, delayed the climb checks and briefly reduced attention to the SID track. SP recognized the saturation, deferred the secondary task and returned to the flying and navigation priorities without IP input. The remaining departure tasks were sequenced correctly.
texts.3: SP managed the departure workload effectively, completing the climb checks and the radio tasks between segment changes and without IP assistance. Priority was kept on flying the aircraft and tracking the published routing. No task was left outstanding at an altitude restriction or turn point.
texts.4: SP sequenced every departure task ahead of the aircraft, completing checks and communications in the quiet portions of each segment so that turns and level-offs required attention only to flying and navigation. Workload remained level throughout the departure with no point of saturation. The entire SID was executed without any IP assistance or prompting.
texts.marginal: SP completed all departure tasks without IP assistance, but several of them were carried out during the turns and level-offs rather than in the segments between, which concentrated the workload at the busiest points. Priorities were nonetheless kept correct and nothing was omitted. Performance meets the standard; SP is expected to plan the task sequence so that checks and calls are completed before the transitions.

texts_at.0: With the IP naming the order of cockpit tasks at the transition, SP worked through the climb checklist and the departure in the order named. The prioritization of the checklist against the flying task at a busy transition has not yet been learned, so the order of actions is still supplied rather than judged independently. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin completing the climb checklist before the first restriction without the order being prompted.
texts_at.1: SP completed the departure tasks only after the IP prompted the order of actions verbally, having saturated at the transition and stopped flying the departure while working the cockpit tasks, with course deviation reaching 8 degrees on the SID track, because the climb checklist had been left unfinished before the first altitude restriction. Progress resumed once the prompting had been given. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to complete the climb checklist before the first restriction without needing the order prompted.
texts_at.2: SP deferred the secondary cockpit task and returned to the flying and navigation priorities without IP input, after a delayed shedding of that task at the segment change had briefly delayed the climb checks and reduced attention to the SID track, letting course deviation grow to about 6 degrees. The remaining departure tasks were sequenced correctly. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to shed the secondary task at the first sign of increasing workload rather than after it has built.
texts_at.3: SP managed the departure workload effectively, completing the climb checks and the radio tasks between segment changes and without IP assistance, keeping priority on flying the aircraft and tracking the published routing within 5 degrees. error_modes.label: Instrument transition and orientation after takeoff

texts.0: SP, due to a delayed instrument transition after entry into cloud on the initial climb, flew on external references that were no longer valid and did not establish the departure attitude on the primary flight instruments. A false attitude perception developed and control inputs were made against the indications presented. IP intervention was required to take the aircraft and re-establish the climb on instruments.
texts.1: SP, due to a false attitude perception in the absence of an external horizon during the first turn, applied bank and pitch that did not match the attitude indicator and allowed the departure profile to reach the limits of the standard. The conflict was resolved only after the IP called the instrument indications verbally. Control on instruments was regained late in the segment.
texts.2: SP, due to an incomplete transition to instruments at the top of the initial climb, briefly flew with attention divided between outside references and the attitude indication, and the departure attitude was held imprecisely. SP recognized the conflict, disregarded the external cues and re-established a full instrument cross-check without IP input. The remainder of the departure was flown on instruments throughout.
texts.3: SP transitioned to instruments at the correct point in the initial climb and maintained the departure attitude from the primary flight instruments. Orientation was maintained through the turns with a cyclic cross-check. No conflict between external cues and the instrument indications was carried into control inputs.
texts.4: SP made the transition to instruments immediately at rotation and flew the entire departure from the primary flight instruments with no reference to external cues. Orientation was maintained through every turn and level-off, and the attitude indication was cross-checked against supporting instruments continuously. The profile showed no sign of any perceptual conflict.
texts.marginal: SP maintained orientation on instruments and flew the departure attitude correctly, but the cross-check narrowed to the attitude indicator during the turns and the supporting instruments were sampled only afterwards. Orientation was never in doubt, though the margin against a perceptual conflict was reduced. The item is within standards; SP is expected to keep the cross-check cyclic across all primary flight instruments during turning flight.

error_modes.label: First turn after takeoff before the 140 KIAS / 700 feet AGL gate

texts.0: SP, due to starting the first turn after takeoff before passing the departure end of the runway, did not attain the minimum 140 KIAS and 700 feet AGL required before turning and rolled in at about 125 KIAS and 500 feet AGL. The early turn placed the aircraft inside the published departure track and course deviation opened beyond 8 degrees. IP intervention on the controls was required to unload the turn and re-establish the climb on the departure course.
texts.1: SP, due to anticipating the departure turn instead of climbing straight ahead as published, began the roll-in just as the aircraft passed the departure end of the runway with airspeed still below 140 KIAS. The gate was not confirmed before bank was applied and course deviation reached the 8 degree limit on the initial radial. The climb attitude and the intercept back to course were re-established only after repeated verbal prompting from the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to an imprecise scan of airspeed and altitude during the initial climb, started the roll-in slightly below 700 feet AGL although the aircraft was already past the departure end of the runway. SP recognized that the gate had not been met, shallowed the bank to protect the rate of climb and held course deviation between 5 and 8 degrees. The turn was completed onto the published radial without IP input.
texts.3: SP climbed straight ahead past the departure end of the runway and delayed the first turn until the aircraft had attained 140 KIAS and 700 feet AGL. The roll-in was made at the published point with course deviation held within 5 degrees. Climb airspeed was maintained through the turn.

texts.marginal: SP met both the 140 KIAS and 700 feet AGL gates before the first turn, but the roll-in followed the gate by only a second or two and the airspeed had barely stabilized. The item is within standards; SP is expected to confirm airspeed and altitude are established before initiating the turn.

error_modes.label: Meeting the published obstacle and ATC climb gradients

texts.0: SP, due to no computation of the required climb gradient during the review of the departure procedure, did not convert the published feet per nautical mile into a pitch attitude and flew the climb at a gradient far below the requirement. The aircraft approached the segment fix several hundred feet under the published crossing altitude and the shortfall was not recognized on the rate of climb against groundspeed. IP intervention was required to set the climb attitude and to advise ATC.
texts.1: SP, due to applying a climb attitude selected by habit rather than from the relationship that 1 degree equals 100 feet per nautical mile, did not meet the published climb gradient and arrived at the restriction fix only just at the crossing altitude. The developing shortfall was not detected in the cross-check, and pitch was increased only after the IP prompted verbally. The remaining segments were flown with continuous prompting on the gradient.
texts.2: SP, due to a groundspeed higher than planned on the departure leg, initially flew a gradient below the published requirement. SP recognized the trend from the rate of climb against groundspeed, increased pitch toward the 10 degree nose-high attitude that yields approximately 1000 feet per nautical mile, and met the crossing restriction without IP input. The gradient was monitored on each subsequent segment.
texts.3: SP computed the required climb gradient during the review of the departure procedure and set the pitch attitude that produces it, using the relationship that 1 degree equals 100 feet per nautical mile. Rate of climb was cross-checked against groundspeed on each segment. Every published crossing restriction was met with altitude in hand.
texts.4: SP converted each published gradient into a pitch attitude before takeoff and set that attitude as soon as the initial climb was established, achieving about 1000 feet per nautical mile at the 10 degree nose-high attitude. Rate of climb against groundspeed was monitored continuously and required no adjustment. All crossing restrictions were met with a wide margin and no change of plan.
texts.marginal: SP met the published obstacle and ATC climb gradients, but the margin at each crossing restriction was small and the required gradient was verified only after the climb was established rather than during the review of the departure procedure. Rate of climb against groundspeed was checked late in each segment. Performance is within standards; SP is expected to compute the gradient before takeoff and set the corresponding pitch attitude from the start of the climb.

texts_at.0: With the IP prompting the pitch increase and naming the feet-per-nautical-mile relationship for the gradient, SP adjusted pitch on the prompting given. The relationship that 1 degree equals 100 feet per nautical mile has not yet been learned well enough to compute the gradient independently, so the climb attitude is still selected by habit until the IP prompts a change. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to begin computing the gradient from the relationship without the pitch increase being prompted.

SP is expected to compute the gradient from the relationship rather than select the attitude by habit.
texts_at.2: SP recognized a shallow-gradient trend from the rate of climb against groundspeed and increased pitch toward the attitude that meets the published gradient, meeting the crossing restriction without IP input after a groundspeed higher than planned had initially produced a gradient below the published requirement. The gradient was then monitored on each subsequent segment. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to check groundspeed against the planned value at the start of the segment so the gradient is set correctly from the outset.
texts_at.3: SP computed the required climb gradient during the review of the departure procedure and set the pitch attitude that produces it, cross-checking rate of climb against groundspeed on each segment so every published crossing restriction was met with altitude in hand. One segment needed a small pitch adjustment once groundspeed settled. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to set the final pitch attitude directly once groundspeed for the segment is known.

error_modes.label: Climb airspeed control and the pitch reduction after reaching climb speed

texts.0: SP, due to failing to lower the nose after reaching the desired climb airspeed, held the initial pitch attitude as altitude increased and allowed airspeed to decay well below the 140-180 KIAS climb band. The high pitch attitude was not reduced and the climb continued with airspeed still decreasing and forward visibility restricted. IP intervention on the controls was required to lower the nose and re-establish the climb airspeed.
texts.1: SP, due to setting the climb pitch attitude once and then leaving it unchanged, climbed out below 160 KIAS at a pitch attitude high enough to limit forward visibility, with airspeed at the lower edge of the climb band. The decay was not detected in the cross-check and the nose was lowered only after the IP called the airspeed. Airspeed was recovered late in the departure segment.
texts.2: SP, due to a pitch attitude set slightly above the value required for the desired airspeed, allowed climb airspeed to drift below 160 KIAS during the first segment. SP identified the trend on the airspeed indicator, lowered the nose in a small increment and returned the aircraft into the 140-180 KIAS band without IP input. Airspeed was then held constant for the rest of the climb.
texts.3: SP accelerated to the climb airspeed within the 140-180 KIAS band and lowered the nose as required to keep airspeed constant as altitude increased. Pitch remained in the normal 10-15 degree range with power set as required. Airspeed was held steady through each departure segment.
texts.4: SP established the climb airspeed and thereafter reduced pitch in small continuous increments, so airspeed remained effectively constant from the initial climb to the level-off. Pitch stayed within the normal 10-15 degree range and forward visibility was never restricted by an excessive attitude. Deviation from the target airspeed was negligible throughout the departure.
texts.marginal: SP kept climb airspeed inside the 140-180 KIAS band, but the nose was lowered only after airspeed had visibly decayed rather than progressively as altitude increased, producing a slow cycle around the target. The resulting pitch corrections were larger than necessary. The parameter is within standards; SP is expected to anticipate the pitch reduction and apply it continuously as the climb progresses.

texts_at.0: With the IP calling the airspeed as it decayed toward the lower edge of the climb band, SP lowered the nose on the call given. The progressive pitch reduction needed as altitude increases has not yet been learned, so the nose is still lowered on a call rather than adjusted continuously through the climb. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to reduce pitch progressively as altitude increases without needing the airspeed called.
texts_at.2: SP identified the decay trend on the airspeed indicator and lowered the nose in a small increment, returning the aircraft into the 140-180 KIAS band without IP input after a pitch attitude set slightly above the required value had let airspeed drift below 160 KIAS during the first segment. error_modes.label: Continuous trimming and trim removal in the rollout from a climbing turn

texts.0: SP, due to not trimming after power was set and the climbing attitude was established, flew the departure against continuous control pressures and did not take out the trim used in the climbing turn during the rollout. The out-of-trim condition carried the aircraft off the departure attitude at rollout and course deviation opened beyond 8 degrees. IP intervention on the controls was required to trim the aircraft and regain the published course.
texts.1: SP, due to treating trim as a single action rather than a continuous process through the climb and level off, held residual turn trim after the rollout and allowed the aircraft to diverge until course deviation reached the 8 degree limit. The control pressure was not associated with the trim setting, and the trim was reset only after the IP pointed it out verbally.
texts.2: SP, due to trim applied in the climbing turn and not removed at the start of the rollout, carried a residual pressure after wings level and drifted off the departure course. SP identified the source of the pressure, trimmed it off and arrested the drift with course deviation between 5 and 8 degrees, without IP input.
texts.3: SP trimmed the aircraft after power was set and the climbing attitude was established, and took out the trim used in each climbing turn during the rollout. Control pressures remained neutral through the departure and course deviation stayed within 5 degrees. Trim was readjusted as airspeed and attitude changed.
texts.4: SP trimmed continuously through the climb, the turns and the level off, so the aircraft was in trim at every stage of the departure and turn trim was taken out progressively during each rollout. No residual control pressure was carried at any point and course deviation remained about 2 degrees. Attitude changes required only light pressures before the trim caught up.
texts.marginal: SP kept the aircraft in trim and removed the turn trim during the rollout, but trimming was done in blocks after each attitude change rather than continuously, so brief out-of-trim pressures were carried between adjustments. Course deviation stayed within 5 degrees throughout. Performance meets the standard; SP is expected to trim as a continuous process through the climb and level off.

texts_at.0: With the IP pointing out the residual turn trim after the rollout, SP reset the trim indicated. error_modes.label: Level-off lead point at the published altitude restrictions

texts.0: SP, due to starting the level-off with no lead point at all, did not lower the nose until the published altitude had already been reached and overshot the restriction by several hundred feet at a high rate of climb. The overshoot was not arrested and the aircraft continued above the assigned altitude. IP intervention on the controls was required to recover to the restriction altitude.
texts.1: SP, due to a lead point chosen without reference to the rate of climb, began the level-off far too late for a climb of about 2000 feet per minute and overshot the published altitude by an amount at the limit of the standard. texts.2: SP, due to a fixed lead point applied regardless of the rate of climb, began the level-off late for the vertical speed being flown and rose slightly above the published altitude. SP recognized the developing overshoot, lowered the nose and returned to the restriction altitude promptly without IP input, then set the PCL for the desired airspeed and trimmed.

The PCL was adjusted to the desired airspeed on approaching it and the aircraft was trimmed. Each restriction altitude was captured without overshoot.
texts.4: SP derived the lead point from the rate of climb at every restriction and started the level-off precisely there, so the transition to level flight was smooth and the altitude was captured with no perceptible overshoot. Power was set for the desired airspeed as the altitude was reached and the aircraft was trimmed immediately. No subsequent altitude correction was needed.
texts.marginal: SP captured each published altitude using a lead point roughly proportional to the rate of climb, but the nose was lowered abruptly at that point rather than smoothly, and power and trim followed a few seconds after level flight. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior level-off lead-point judgment.

error_modes.label: Emergency return plan and contingency review for the departure

texts.0: SP, due to a review of the departure procedure that omitted the surrounding terrain, hazards and the plan for emergency return, had no approach plate for the primary recovery approach available and no course of action for problems before or after gear retraction. When an immediate return to the departure base was postulated, SP could state neither the recovery approach nor the no radio procedure. IP assistance was required to supply the plan and to fly the aircraft.
texts.1: SP, due to a contingency review limited to reading the departure routing, had not developed a specific course of action for each section of the departure and could not describe the emergency recovery until the plate was located in flight. The primary recovery approach was identified only after the IP prompted for it verbally, and the departure was flown while the plan was reconstructed.
texts.2: SP, due to an emergency return plan built for the departure as a whole rather than for each section of it, hesitated when the course of action after gear retraction in IMC was queried. SP referred to the recovery approach plate that had been kept available, stated the plan correctly and continued the departure without IP assistance.
texts.3: SP reviewed the entire departure procedure including surrounding terrain, hazards and climb gradient requirements, and kept the approach plate for the primary recovery approach open and available. A course of action existed for each section of the departure and the no radio procedure was known. The plan was stated without hesitation when queried.
texts.4: SP briefed the departure with terrain, hazards, climb gradient requirements and the no radio procedure covered in full, and had a specific course of action ready for problems before gear retraction, after gear retraction in VMC and in IMC. The primary recovery approach was displayed and the effect of the surrounding terrain on the recovery was described. Every contingency query was answered immediately and correctly.
texts.marginal: SP had an emergency return plan and the recovery approach plate available, but the effect of terrain on the recovery and the no radio procedure were recalled only after a pause when queried. The plan covered the departure adequately and no IP assistance was needed. Performance is within standards; SP is expected to develop a course of action for each section of the departure so the contingency answers are immediate.

texts_at.0: With the IP prompting for the primary recovery approach and pointing to the plate in flight, SP stated the approach named. The habit of building a specific course of action for each section of the departure has not yet been formed, so the recovery approach is still located in flight rather than planned before takeoff. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to begin building a specific course of action for each section of the departure before takeoff.
texts_at.1: SP stated the primary recovery approach only after the IP prompted for it verbally, having been unable to describe the emergency recovery until the plate was located in flight, because the contingency review had been limited to reading the departure routing. The departure was flown while the plan was reconstructed until the prompting was given. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to build a specific course of action for each section of the departure before takeoff.
texts_at.2: SP referred to the recovery approach plate that had been kept available and stated the plan correctly without IP assistance, after an emergency return plan built for the departure as a whole rather than by section had left a brief hesitation when the course of action after gear retraction in IMC was queried. The departure continued without further hesitation. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to build the plan section by section so no query produces a pause.
texts_at.3: SP reviewed the entire departure procedure including surrounding terrain, hazards and climb gradient requirements, and kept the approach plate for the primary recovery approach open and available, with a course of action for each section of the departure and the no radio procedure known. The plan for one section was stated after a brief pause rather than immediately. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to bring every section to the same immediacy as the fastest one.

texts_above.1: SP stated the primary recovery approach and flew the departure once the contingency plan had been reconstructed. That correction came after a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP referred to the recovery approach plate that had been kept available and stated the plan correctly without IP assistance, after an emergency return plan built for the departure as a whole had produced a brief hesitation on one query about gear retraction in IMC. No further hesitation followed. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent departure contingency planning.
texts_above.3: SP reviewed the entire departure procedure including surrounding terrain, hazards and climb gradient requirements and kept the primary recovery approach plate open and available, with a specific course of action for every section of the departure and the no radio procedure known and stated without hesitation. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed departure contingency planning.
texts_above.4: SP briefed the departure with terrain, hazards, climb gradient requirements and the no radio procedure covered in full, with a specific course of action ready for problems before gear retraction, after gear retraction in VMC and in IMC, and every contingency query answered immediately and correctly. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional departure contingency planning.

error_modes.label: Readiness for departure routing and altitude changes

texts.0: SP, due to planning a routing other than the preferred routing and to no review of the departure routing and altitude restrictions before takeoff, was unprepared for the amended clearance and continued to fly the original plan after departure. The change of routing and altitude was never incorporated and the aircraft diverged from the assigned track by more than 8 degrees. IP intervention was required to reset the navigation and to fly the amended departure.
texts.1: SP, due to reliance on a single planned routing with no alternatives reviewed, lost the picture when the departure routing was changed while on departure and stopped flying the published track while reconstructing the clearance. The amended routing was set up only after the IP prompted the actions verbally, by which time deviation from the assigned track had reached the 8 degree limit.
texts.2: SP, due to an altitude restriction review completed only for the originally planned routing, was slow to accept the amended departure clearance and briefly continued toward the previous fix. SP compared the amendment against the plate, re-set the navigation and rejoined the assigned routing without IP assistance, holding deviation between 5 and 8 degrees.
texts.3: SP planned preferred routings where applicable and reviewed the departure routing and altitude restrictions before takeoff, so the clearance issued required no significant change of plan. An amendment received on departure was incorporated without loss of situational awareness and the assigned track was held within 5 degrees.
texts.4: SP planned the preferred routing and reviewed the alternative routings and altitude restrictions before takeoff, so the amendment issued on departure was anticipated and applied at once with the navigation already set for it. Situational awareness was maintained throughout and the assigned track was held to about 2 degrees. No element of the original plan had to be reconstructed in flight.
texts.marginal: SP incorporated the amended departure routing correctly, but the alternatives had not been reviewed before takeoff and the change was worked out in flight while the aircraft was in the turn. The assigned track stayed within 5 degrees and no assistance was required. The item is within standards; SP is expected to plan preferred routings and review the likely alternatives so amendments demand no in-flight reconstruction.

texts_at.0: With the IP prompting the actions needed to set up the amended routing, SP flew the amendment on the prompting given. The review of a likely alternative routing has not yet become a habit, so an amendment still costs the picture until the IP prompts the setup. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to begin reviewing at least one likely alternative before takeoff without the setup being prompted.
texts_at.1: SP set up the amended routing only after the IP prompted the actions verbally, with deviation from the assigned track reaching the 8 degree limit, because reliance on a single planned routing had left the picture lost when the departure routing changed on departure. The assigned routing was rejoined once the prompting had been given. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to review at least one likely alternative before takeoff so an amendment does not lose the picture.
texts_at.2: SP compared the amendment against the plate, re-set the navigation and rejoined the assigned routing without IP assistance, holding deviation to about 7 degrees, after an altitude-restriction review completed only for the originally planned routing had left the acceptance of the amended clearance slow. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to review the amendment against the plate the moment it is issued rather than after a brief continuation on the previous fix.
texts_at.3: SP planned preferred routings where applicable and reviewed the departure routing and altitude restrictions before takeoff, so an amendment received on departure was incorporated without loss of situational awareness and the assigned track held within 5 degrees. The amendment took a moment longer to absorb than the planned routing itself. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to review one likely alternative before takeoff so an amendment absorbs as quickly as the planned routing.

texts_above.1: SP set up the amended routing and rejoined the assigned track, containing deviation to the 8 degree limit. The IP's verbal call preceded the correction. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP compared an amended clearance against the plate, re-set the navigation and rejoined the assigned routing without IP assistance, holding deviation between 5 and 8 degrees after an altitude-restriction review limited to the original routing had slowed the initial acceptance. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid routing-amendment readiness.
texts_above.3: SP planned preferred routings where applicable and reviewed the departure routing and altitude restrictions before takeoff on every departure, so an amendment received on departure was incorporated without loss of situational awareness and the assigned track held within 5 degrees. No amendment on the departure needed the picture rebuilt. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate routing-amendment readiness.
texts_above.4: SP planned the preferred routing and reviewed the alternative routings and altitude restrictions before takeoff, so an amendment issued on departure was anticipated and applied at once with the navigation already set for it, holding the assigned track to about 2 degrees with no element of the original plan reconstructed in flight. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary routing-amendment readiness.

error_modes.label: Acceleration and climb rate control on the climbout to the radar pattern

texts.0: SP, due to leaving power set as for the departure climb after the transition from the departure leg, did not reduce the PCL to control acceleration and climb rate when entering the radar pattern and allowed airspeed to run well above the 160-200 KIAS band. The aircraft arrived on radar downwind fast and above the assigned altitude. IP intervention on the controls was required to reduce power and stabilize the pattern entry.
texts.1: SP, due to a power reduction made only after the airspeed had already increased, allowed acceleration and climb rate to go unchecked on the climbout and reached the upper edge of the 160-200 KIAS band before the aircraft was under control in the pattern. The airspeed trend was not detected in the cross-check and power was reduced only after the IP called it verbally. 200 KIAS on radar downwind was regained late.
texts.2: SP, due to late anticipation of the climbout power requirement, accelerated above the target before reducing the PCL when entering the radar pattern. SP recognized the trend on the airspeed indicator, reduced power and stabilized the aircraft inside the 160-200 KIAS band without IP input. 200 KIAS was then held on radar downwind and 160 KIAS set on radar base.
texts.3: SP reduced power as required to control acceleration and climb rate on entering the radar pattern and maintained airspeed inside the 160-200 KIAS band. 200 KIAS was held on radar downwind and the aircraft was slowed to 160 KIAS on radar base. The transition from the departure leg was flown without airspeed excursions.
texts.4: SP anticipated the power reduction so that acceleration and climb rate were controlled from the moment the aircraft entered the radar pattern, with airspeed held on the target values throughout. 200 KIAS on radar downwind and 160 KIAS on radar base were captured without overshoot and held to within a few knots. Neither leg required a further power adjustment.
texts.marginal: SP held the climbout airspeed inside the 160-200 KIAS band and set 200 KIAS on radar downwind and 160 KIAS on radar base, but each target was captured by a late power reduction after the airspeed had drifted toward the edge of the band. Climb rate control followed the same pattern. The parameter is within standards; SP is expected to lead the power changes so that the airspeed is captured rather than caught.

texts_at.0: With the IP calling the airspeed trend on the climbout to the radar pattern, SP reduced power on the call given. The detection of an accelerating trend on the climbout has not yet been learned, so power is still reduced on a call rather than in response to the trend seen on the cross-check. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin detecting the acceleration trend without the airspeed being called.
texts_at.1: SP regained the 200 KIAS radar-downwind target only after the IP called it verbally, with the airspeed trend not detected in the cross-check before the aircraft entered the upper edge of the 160-200 KIAS band, because power had been reduced only after the airspeed had already increased. The pattern entry stabilized once the call had been given. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to detect the acceleration trend without needing the airspeed called.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the accelerating trend on the airspeed indicator and reduced power to stabilize inside the 160-200 KIAS band without IP input, after late anticipation of the climbout power requirement had let the aircraft accelerate above the target before entering the radar pattern. 200 KIAS was then held on radar downwind and 160 KIAS set on radar base. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to anticipate the power reduction before entering the pattern rather than after the acceleration is under way.
texts_at.3: SP reduced power as required to control acceleration and climb rate on entering the radar pattern and maintained airspeed inside the 160-200 KIAS band, holding 200 KIAS on radar downwind and slowing to 160 KIAS on radar base with the transition flown without airspeed excursions. One power reduction was made a moment later than the others. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to lead every climbout power reduction with the same anticipation as the earliest one.

texts_above.1: SP reduced power and regained the 200 KIAS radar-downwind target once the airspeed trend had been called. A verbal call from the IP came before the correction. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized an accelerating trend on the airspeed indicator and reduced power to stabilize inside the 160-200 KIAS band without IP input, after late anticipation of the climbout power requirement had let the aircraft run above the target briefly on entering the radar pattern. 200 KIAS was held on radar downwind once stabilized. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good climbout power management into the radar pattern.
texts_above.3: SP reduced power as required to control acceleration and climb rate on every entry into the radar pattern, holding airspeed inside the 160-200 KIAS band with 200 KIAS on radar downwind and 160 KIAS on radar base and no airspeed excursion on the transition. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed climbout power management into the radar pattern.
texts_above.4: SP anticipated the power reduction so acceleration and climb rate were controlled from the moment the aircraft entered the radar pattern, capturing 200 KIAS on radar downwind and 160 KIAS on radar base without overshoot and holding each to within a few knots with neither leg needing a further power adjustment. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional climbout power management into the radar pattern.
